Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making eye contact with other people
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette: Maya, a thirty‑year‑old bank teller married to her college sweetheart, remembers the day she was dragged into a basement by men in uniform as a nightmare that never lets go. The memory is so vivid that she can feel the damp concrete under her feet, the metallic clang of the door, the echoing hiss of orders. When that memory surfaces, it floods her senses with the same intensity it had on the night, so she often stops mid‑sentence, eyes glazing over, because the overwhelm forces her to retreat from her own thoughts. She reports that even the slightest expression of anger in the hallway—a cashier’s raised voice, a manager’s clipped admonition—triggers the full sensory reliving of that night, sending her heart racing and her skin prickling. Those angry outbursts do more than remind her of the past; they ignite a threat response that leaves her feeling jumpy, as if something dangerous is lurking in the shadows of the bank’s fluorescent lights. The sense of being watched, the unspoken gaze of a fellow teller, or the quiet hush that follows a loud argument all act as cues that she is in danger, amplifying her startle and making her wake at night to check whether she is safe. The triggers, therefore, do not simply remind her of trauma; they trigger the very threat states she has learned to anticipate. The relentless threat perception, in turn, drives Maya’s coping habits. To keep herself from feeling the sting of the bank’s fluorescent glare, she has learned to avoid eye contact with anyone who might be looking at her, fearing that a glance will betray her vulnerability. She spends hours on her phone after work, scrolling through articles about safety, overanalyzing every subtle shift in the office’s atmosphere. When the memory floods her, she feels compelled to retreat into compulsive spending—she buys items on the spot, hoping the purchase will quiet the frantic buzz inside her. Each act of impulsive buying provides a brief, but hollow, sense of control; yet the act itself reinforces her anxiety, because it reminds her of the helplessness she felt in the basement. Her maladaptive strategies become both a shield and a trigger: the avoidance of eye contact makes her feel isolated, prompting her to search for reassurance online, which feeds back into the memory loop. These strategies feed directly back into the memory, making the recall more intense each time she engages in them, and they also heighten her sense of threat, perpetuating the startle response even when nothing is amiss. In the weeks that followed the trauma, the full sensory reliving of the basement seeped into everyday moments. The quiet of the night air during a family dinner or the sudden silence in a crowded lunch room made Maya feel as though danger was looming. Even the suggestion of intimacy—a partner’s tentative touch or a conversation about future plans—sent a rush of panic, reminding her of the violence that had once been her world. Each of these events triggers the memory, which then floods her with terror, which in turn compels her to avoid eye contact, to overanalyze, to shop compulsively. When she finds herself in a corner of the bank watching a customer with a suspicious expression, she feels a sudden startle and her body tightens; the sense of being watched is almost a reflex, a threat that makes her want to leave the bank at the next opportunity. Maya’s relationship has suffered because of her avoidance. Her husband, concerned about her anxiety, has asked her to attend a counseling session together, but she feels that any discussion about “what happened” will only amplify the memory. She fears that if she lets herself talk, the memory will return with the same ferocity, and she will lose herself again in the overwhelm. She also worries that if she stops buying small things—her latest impulse purchases—she will feel even more exposed and vulnerable. This creates a vicious cycle: the more she resists, the more the memory resurfaces, the more she turns to maladaptive strategies to keep the threat at bay. The decision to seek help came after a night of waking repeatedly, each time checking the bathroom mirror to ensure her reflection was ordinary, not distorted. She realized that the pattern had become a part of her identity, shaping how she approached her job, her marriage, and even her own sense of self. What most frightens her is the possibility that the memory might return in an even more unhinged form, and what she hopes for most is a way to quiet the internal alarm without sacrificing the life she has built around her bank teller desk and her husband’s steady support.
